text: Around 3150 BC, Pharaoh Menes, identified by many with Narmer, achieved the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt, consolidating a centralized state and giving rise to the first pharaonic dynasty. The Egyptian Empire as a unified civilization spanned more than 3,000 years, from unification around 3100 BC to the Roman conquest in 31 BC. This extensive history is divided into three major imperial periods of apogee (Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms), interspersed with periods of instability and foreign domination. Key Periods:
Unification (c. 3100 BC):
The beginning of Egyptian civilization is marked by the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt by Pharaoh Menes.
Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BC):
Known for the construction of the great pyramids and a golden age of pharaonic power.
Middle Kingdom (c. 2055–1750 BC):
Marked by expansion and subsequent cession of power to the Hyksos.
New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BC):
The era of great pharaohs like Ramses II, where Egypt reached its greatest expansion.
End of the unified civilization (31 BC):
Egypt, after a period of decline, was conquered by the Romans, ending its independence as an empire.
